text:
Tens of thousands of unaccompanied minors may soon face deportation without proper representation, their legal advocates said at a press briefing Tuesday.

The federal government’s contract with the Acacia Center for Justice, a national legal services organization, expires July 31. But its lawyers say the Trump administration has not provided any guidance on how cases involving children who enter the country alone will be handled after that, and they haven’t been paid since November.

Acacia Justice Center Executive Director Shaina Aber said the administration’s ultimate goal is to expel the children.

“Abandoning children to meet arbitrary mass deportation targets is immoral,” Aber said at the virtual press conference. “Children facing this system deserve legal representation and to have their voices heard.”

A request for comment to the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services was not returned by press time.

Former deputy chief immigration judge in San Francisco Elizabeth Young — one of at least 130 immigration judges fired by the Trump administration — was among those speaking out at Tuesday’s press conference. She said when a child has no lawyer, there is no one to explain legal standards, gather evidence and identify forms of relief — and thus there is no way for the child to meaningfully understand what is happening in court. She said immigration cases involving kids who do not appear with an attorney decreases the likelihood they will successfully argue their cases and threatens the credibility of courts.

“When children are forced to navigate one of the most complex areas of law alone, that promise of fairness becomes little more than an illusion,” Young said. “A legal system that values fairness cannot expect children to carry that burden alone.”

Known as unaccompanied minors, children who enter the country without a parent or guardian are typically fleeing violence, abuse and exploitation. Roughly 90% arrive from Mexico or Central America, according to the most recent data from the Office of Refugee Resettlement, the federal agency responsible for their care.

These youth have faced precarious prospects during the second Trump administration. In May 2025, the federal government challenged the decades-old Flores settlement agreement, which requires the federal government to hold children in safe, sanitary conditions and release them to relatives without unnecessary delay.

“When children are forced to navigate one of the most complex areas of law alone, that promise of fairness becomes little more than an illusion. A legal system that values fairness cannot expect children to carry that burden alone.”

—Elizabeth Young, Former deputy chief immigration judge in California

Children now remain in custody for months on end, and they are far less likely to be released to vetted family members than in years past, according to a report by the Acacia Center for Justice released last year.

Legal protections for migrant kids became an early target of the Trump administration.

In March 2025, the Department of Health and Human Services abruptly terminated Acacia’s $200 million contract to provide legal aid to more than 20,000 unaccompanied minors. The Washington, D.C.-based nonprofit subcontracts with more than 100 organizations to represent youth and provide legal clinics at detention facilities.

Later that year, the federal government required that the children’s lawyers turn over sensitive information about their clients. When they refused, their funding was frozen, leaving many legal aid groups serving immigrant youth struggling to operate. According to Aber, many firms are weighing layoffs, hiring freezes or closure.

The Texas-based Estrella del Paso, for example, is seeking donations because it has not received up to $765,000 in federal payments. The nonprofit is facing closure after 40 years, the El Paso Times reported last week.

Losing a legal right to representation?

Migrant kids who arrive without a parent or guardian receive special protections since passage of the Trafficking Victims Protection Reauthorization Act of 2008. While the law doesn’t guarantee a lawyer, it said the government should help facilitate access to legal counsel. Several different federal and state programs fund legal representation for some migrant children via grants to legal organizations, according to the American Civil Liberties Union.

Unlike the criminal legal system, defendants in immigration court are not guaranteed a court-appointed attorney. But the 2008 law acknowledged that children — especially those looking to escape political, ethnic or religious persecution, or abuse — are uniquely vulnerable. In court documents, attorneys who represent these children have described the reasons migrant kids are unable to navigate the complex immigration system on their own: their age, a lack of English skills and the depth of their trauma.

A coalition of legal providers and immigrant rights groups sued the administration to reinstate the Acacia contract in April 2025, and won temporary relief. The still-pendinglitigation is moving through the courts.

Since then, the administration has issued a series of three-month funding extensions for the unaccompanied minors program while the lawsuit proceeds.

But earlier this month, the Texas Tribune revealed what may be the federal government’s next step. The online outlet reported that the Texas Indigent Defense Commission, which provides criminal defense for low-income residents, had been contacted by Trump administration officials about the possibility of providing legal services to migrant children.

On July 16, 13 Democratic lawmakers from Texas objected to such a move. In a letter to Department of Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. and Office of Refugee Resettlement Acting Director Angie Salazar, they said ending Acacia’s contract “would result in an alarming number of children potentially having no representation at an immigration hearing or feeling pressured to voluntarily depart the country.”

The lawmakers urged the administration to “release the overdue funds to the legal service providers that are already providing these children with the legal representation they not only need, but are legally required to receive.”

text:
HITCHCOCK, Texas (KTRK) -- A proposal to bring Hitchcock Police into a federal immigration partnership is off the table.

Monday night, city council members voted down an agreement with the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement that would have expanded the department's role in immigration enforcement.

A three-to-two vote stopped Hitchcock from joining the 287(g) program, which is a partnership that would have trained more than a dozen officers to work alongside ICE after local criminal arrests.

According to ICE, there are more than 2,100 participating law enforcement agencies across the country.

The Hitchcock agenda item said 16 law enforcement officers would've been trained as 287g task force officers.

"So what does that look like? It looks like during the course of normal investigations or criminal law investigations, an officer if they believe that someone is here illegally, then they can contact the Department of Homeland Security to confirm the residency status," Assistant Chief Jeff Evans said.

Evans highlighted incentives tied to the partnership.

"The federal government has allocated for each partner agency $100,000 per year for related expenses, $7,500 per officer," he said. "We would also have access to reimbursement of funds for time spent while on call."

Some council members said they see the benefit of training local police in this way.

"They have a better rapport with the citizens, and it's handled in a more humane way rather than strangers coming in here and doing what they do," Councilmember Brian Smith said.

Others, like Councilmember Mary Combs Demby, said they couldn't justify the program.

"I understand that this department is underfunded and the officers underpaid, but I truly believe this is not the way to do it," Combs Demby said.

This discussion comes less than two weeks after two fatal shootings involving ICE agents. One of them was in Houston and involved 52-year-old Lorenzo Salgado Araujo.

DHS claimed Salgado Araujo was evading arrest and allegedly rammed his car into an ICE vehicle. However, at this moment, there's no video released showing that. DHS also said the agents involved were not wearing body cameras.

Those events were ultimately top of mind as council weighed the proposal.

"Whatever amount of money that the city gets is not worth anybody's life," Combs Demby said. "We have seen what has gone on with ICE."

title: ICE detains Chicago Public Schools custodian at immigration appointment
description:
His father, Josue Pire Hidalgo, had been taken aside and sent to the ICE processing center earlier that day.
“He was the one translating because my English is bad,” said the boy’s mother, the wife of Pire Hidalgo.
Now, a North Side community is rallying around Pire Hidalgo, a Chicago Public Schools custodian and father of two, whose arrest comes as immigration enforcement has surged across the Midwest this summer.
Pire Hidalgo’s wife said the family almost skipped the appointment after friends warned them not to go.
Especially as she prepares for her own immigration hearing scheduled for next year.
text:
A 13-year-old Venezuelan boy tried to stay calm as he translated the words his mother could not understand during their immigration check-in on Friday morning.

Standing inside a small room in an Immigration and Customs Enforcement office in downtown Chicago, he began to cry after he was told to tell his mother that the entire family was being detained. His father, Josue Pire Hidalgo, had been taken aside and sent to the ICE processing center earlier that day.

“He was the one translating because my English is bad,” said the boy’s mother, the wife of Pire Hidalgo. “When my son heard that I was detained, he became very nervous. He started crying.”

When an interpreter was eventually called because the boy could no longer translate, the woman was told that she and her children would be released because their 6-year-old daughter has asthma and relies on daily medication, but the mother would be required to wear an ankle monitor.

Now, a North Side community is rallying around Pire Hidalgo, a Chicago Public Schools custodian and father of two, whose arrest comes as immigration enforcement has surged across the Midwest this summer. Attorneys and immigrant advocates say ICE has increasingly begun to target people during routine immigration check-ins, in criminal courthouse parking lots and during traffic stops — a shift from the large-scale workplace raids and neighborhood operations that dominated headlines a year ago.

CPS said in a statement to the Tribune that the district ensures that all new hires hold legal authorization to work in the U.S. in accordance with federal, state and municipal laws, and that it also “provides support and resources to international employees when immigration issues arise.” According to CPS records, Pire Hidalgo has worked as a custodian in the district since July 2025, most recently at Farnsworth Elementary School in Jefferson Park.

CPS did not respond to further questions after its statement, explaining it does not disclose personnel information due to “privacy practices.”

Pire Hidalgo’s wife said the family arrived downtown the morning of July 17 for what they believed would be a routine ICE appointment for their asylum case, an appointment they had waited more than three years to attend. They entered the United States in late 2022, applied for asylum, obtained work permits and secured jobs as CPS custodians.

“We thought we were doing everything the right way,” said his wife, who the Tribune is not naming because she fears retribution. “We don’t have a deportation order. We don’t have any crimes. We pay taxes. We work for the state. We always tried to follow the law. I never imagined this would happen.”

A public records search in Cook and suburban counties did not immediately reveal any criminal history for a man with the same name. A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security said the department would not be able to provide immediate comment.

Pire Hidalgo’s wife said the family almost skipped the appointment after friends warned them not to go. Instead, they decided complying with the law was their safest option.

“I told him, ‘Let’s follow the law,'” she said. “‘If we don’t show up, it could be worse. Let’s keep going with our process.'”

Instead, she said, the appointment ended with her husband in ICE custody, their family separated for the first time in their 17 years together. He’s now being held at a jail in Clay County, Indiana. His next hearing is scheduled for July 28, his wife said.

“He’s a very good father, a very hard worker and a very good husband,” she said. “He’s always taken care of us. This is the first time we’ve ever been separated, and it’s been very hard for me and for our children.”

Their children attend a CPS school on the city’s North Side, and neighbors and the school community are now scrambling to support the family. A GoFundMe created to help support them had raised nearly $15,000 Monday night. A parent-led mutual aid network created last school year to support immigrant families during Operation Midway Blitz is poised to organize meal trains, collect clothing and distribute food and other necessities, parents said.

“I think the community is really trying to rally around them,” said Angeline Groves, a founder of the network. “My youngest is the same age as their youngest. They go to school together, and this is one of my daughter’s friends that this is happening to.”

Anna Duski, another school parent, recalled the quiet routines that have become familiar over the past year for her and her children, who have gotten to know the family as they navigate the uncertainty of the immigration system.

“They’re very sweet, close-knit children,” she said. “The brother would walk the sister into school in the mornings and hold her hand. He goes to a different door just to walk her in and then goes back to the entrance where the older kids go.”

She said the family has become deeply woven into the neighborhood through their jobs and their children’s school.

“They’re valuable members of our community,” she said. “The kids are friends with our kids. The family is just trying to provide a better life for their kids, and I think they are heroes.”

She added: “Everyone’s just devastated that this happened to them.”

SEIU Local 73, which represents public sector employees in Illinois and northwest Indiana, including some CPS custodians and nonteacher employees, said in a statement that it stands behind Pire Hidalgo and is organizing its members and communities to demand his immediate release.

“Chicago is a city built by people like Josue Pire Hidalgo — people who show up before sunrise to open our schools, who keep the hallways clean and the classrooms safe, so that every child, no matter their zip code or their parents’ paperwork, has a decent place to learn,” SEIU Local 73 Executive Vice President Trumaine Reeves said in the statement.

Reeves added that more widely, the union is fighting for a city “where a man can go to a scheduled appointment and come home to his family that night” and “no child has to wonder if their custodian, their neighbor, or their parent will be there when they get home.”

“That is the city we are building, together, and we will not stop until Josue Pire Hidalgo is back where he belongs — home, with his family, and back on the job serving the students of Chicago,” Reeves said.

Pire Hidalgo’s wife said she worries about her husband being in detention because he was born with hearing loss in both ears. He cannot hear out of one ear and has very limited hearing in the other. After arriving in the United States, he underwent medical evaluations and was prescribed hearing aids, which he has used for about four years, she said.

While her husband was taken into custody with his hearing aids, he doesn’t have a charger in detention. She worries the lack of access to his devices could affect his ability to participate in his immigration proceedings, especially since his next hearing is expected to take place by video.

“I’m afraid he won’t hear well,” she said. “People tend to misunderstand when someone has to ask for things to be repeated several times. He either reads lips or gets closer to the person speaking so he can understand.”

But she said she draws strength from the community that has rallied around her family. Especially as she prepares for her own immigration hearing scheduled for next year.

“I’m trusting God,” she said. “I’m doing everything I possibly can, and the support from the community, moral, emotional and financial, has given me the strength to keep fighting for him.”

She said her husband’s colleagues describe him as a dedicated employee and a valued member of the school community. He has worked for CPS for about a year, while she has worked there slightly longer, she said. Their jobs allowed them to provide for their children while they continued their legal case.

“He is very, very loved at his school,” his wife said. “He is a very good worker. We are always well evaluated. They have no complaints about us. We like what we do, and we value our work.”

Chicago Tribune’s Tess Kenny contributed.

name: Human Rights
title: Immigration - Immigration judge failed to follow law - Virginia Lawyers Weekly
description:
Where an immigration judge failed to follow the required two-step process when considering whether a petitioner was eligible for asylum and withholding of removal, the decision was vacated.
Background Warner Odir Guevara Martinez entered the United States without authorization.
Seeking relief from removal, Guevara Martinez applied for asylum, withholding of removal and protection from removal under the Convention Against Torture, or CAT.
An immigration judge, or IJ, first found Guevara Martinez not credible.
Dissenting opinion Wilkinson, J., dissenting: Guevara Martinez illegally entered the United States.
text:
Where an immigration judge failed to follow the required two-step process when considering whether a petitioner was eligible for asylum and withholding of removal, the decision was vacated.

Background

Warner Odir Guevara Martinez entered the United States without authorization. Seeking relief from removal, Guevara Martinez applied for asylum, withholding of removal and protection from removal under the Convention Against Torture, or CAT.

An immigration judge, or IJ, first found Guevara Martinez not credible. On the claims for asylum and withholding of removal, the IJ concluded that Guevara Martinez was statutorily ineligible because he had previously been convicted of a “particularly serious crime.”

The IJ also denied protection under the CAT, finding that Guevara Martinez failed to show a sufficient likelihood that he would be tortured if he returned to El Salvador. The Board of Immigration Appeals, or BIA, affirmed the IJ’s order in full.

Jurisdiction

The government argues that because the ultimate determination of the applicability of the particularly serious crime bar is “an unbounded judgment call,” this court is precluded from reviewing the reasoning of the IJ. Not so. Even if the ultimate determination of applicability of the particularly serious crime bar was a “discretionary determination[ ] of the BIA are not subject to review,” the court would “[n]evertheless[ ] . . . retain jurisdiction to review . . . questions of law” de novo.

Particularly serious crime

IJs are required to apply a two-step test to ask: “(1) whether the elements of the offense bring it within the ambit of a particularly serious crime; and if so, (2) whether the individual facts and circumstances confirm that the offense is particularly serious.” These steps must be taken in order, with the elements of the crime evaluated before consideration of the facts.

On the first step, the IJ did not meaningfully analyze the elements of the crime of assault and battery against a family member under Virginia law. Instead, the IJ concluded summarily, without reasoning, that “the elements of the offense fall within the ambit of a particularly serious crime.”

The IJ then proceeded to step two and described the facts of Guevara Martinez’s 2023 conviction in detail. After describing these facts, the IJ concluded that “[b]ecause the statute of conviction is a crime against a person, the elements ‘potentially bring the crime within the ambit of a particularly serious crime.’”

The relevant caselaw makes clear that such analysis cannot suffice. The IJ did not sufficiently explain why the elements of assault and battery against a family member under Virginia law fall within the ambit of a particularly serious crime. Even the limited analysis offered by the IJ—noting that the statute of conviction involves a crime against a person—came too late. The IJ made this observation only after a prolonged discussion of the particular facts of this case, contrary to the order required by BIA precedent. The IJ’s swapping of steps was improper. The BIA’s decision is vacated and remanded for further proceedings consistent with this opinion.

Remaining arguments

Although Guevara Martinez also challenges the determination that he is not credible, it is abundantly clear that the IJ’s adverse credibility determination here was supported by substantial evidence. Finally, while Guevera Martinez contends that the IJ erred in concluding that he was not entitled to relief under the CAT, the IJ’s findings were supported by substantial evidence.

Petition for review granted in part, denied in part; order vacated and remanded.

Dissenting opinion

Wilkinson, J., dissenting: Guevara Martinez illegally entered the United States. When the government sought to remove him, he requested asylum and withholding of removal. The IJ and BIA denied relief, and for good reason: His version of events is in equal parts extraordinary and preposterous, featuring the haphazard trafficking of human hearts, a divine intervention at the brink of death and a Terminator-style motorcycle chase.

He also paints himself as the misunderstood victim in his own convictions for throwing his partner to the ground by her hair, punching the back of her head, threatening to rip out her contraceptive implant, repeatedly blocking her efforts for help and trying to abscond with their daughter.

The majority disputes none of this. Yet it vacates and remands anyway, claiming the agency failed to properly apply its own case law when determining whether Guevara Martinez’s domestic violence qualified as a “particularly serious crime.” Since his tall tales already doom his asylum and withholding claims, it is simply not relevant what kind of crime he committed. Even if it were somehow relevant, the IJ and BIA correctly concluded from the factual record that Guevara Martinez’s brutal assault on a family member was a particularly serious crime.

Guevara Martinez v. Blanche, Case No. 25-1429, July 7, 2026. 4th Cir. (Berner), from Board of Immigration Appeals. Ariel Alyssa Rosenbaum for Petitioner. Jesse David Lorenz for Respondent. VLW 026-248. 35 pp.

text:
A federal judge has blocked the Trump administration’s policies that imposed new hurdles to asylum applications and revoked work authorizations for people with Temporary Protected Status (TPS). The emergency order issued Tuesday, July 21 by U.S. District Judge Nathaniel Gorton provides temporary relief for thousands of immigrants who still hold valid work permits and will remain in effect until August 5, when the judge is expected to decide whether to maintain the suspension of those measures in the long term.

The ruling responds to a lawsuit filed by a coalition of immigrant-rights organizations seeking to challenge several immigration measures included in the Big, Beautiful Bill Act, passed by Congress and signed by Trump in July 2025. Among the contested provisions are the imposition of fees for asylum applications and the elimination of employment authorizations for TPS beneficiaries from countries affected by war, natural disasters, and conflict that prevents their return home.

“The court’s decision ensures that thousands of families will not lose their livelihoods or peace of mind while the legality of these policies is determined,” said Skye Perryman, president and CEO of Democracy Forward, one of the organizations that filed the suit. Democracy Forward said in a statement: “Without this emergency intervention, many TPS beneficiaries would have been unable to work as of July 22, 2026, while asylum seekers faced denials of their applications and immediate termination of their employment authorization.”

In practice, the emergency order benefits asylum applicants from all countries and, particularly, TPS beneficiaries from Haiti and Venezuela.

“The most important aspect of this decision is its impact on asylum seekers who had pending cases and who were about to lose their work authorization or even face expedited removal for failing to pay the new annual $100 fee imposed by the Trump administration,” activist Adelys Ferro, executive director of the NGO Venezuelan American Caucus, told EL PAÍS. She added that these people will now have the opportunity to pay the required fee and continue their cases while retaining work authorization.

Meanwhile, Haitian immigrants with TPS who faced the loss of their work permits on July 24 will be able to keep them until November 2026. That is when the most recent renewal of Temporary Protected Status for Haitian nationals, approved by the Biden administration, expires.

For Venezuelan immigrants, the relief applies only to a small group of beneficiaries who filed to renew their TPS before February 5, 2025, and whose work permits were valid through October 2026. According to the Venezuelan American Caucus’s estimates, between 5,000 and 10,000 Venezuelans still hold that status and could benefit from the emergency order.

So far, lower courts are the only ones to have pushed back against Trump’s immigration agenda. Although several lower courts have ruled against him repeatedly, the president has often had the backing of the Supreme Court for some of his most contentious initiatives, such as ending temporary protections for people fleeing countries in turmoil and limiting the number of people who may seek asylum, among other measures.

text:
A federal judge in Texas this week temporarily barred immigration authorities from deporting one of the witnesses in the fatal shooting of Mexican immigrant Lorenzo Salgado Araujo by Immigration and Customs Enforcement earlier this month in Houston.

U.S. District Judge Keith Ellison issued an order Monday blocking ICE from deporting Jose Trinidad Rojas Pliego without first getting the judge's permission. Ellison also barred ICE from transferring Rojas Pliego away from the Southern District of Texas without prior approval.

Rojas Pliego, who is facing deportation proceedings, is one of three construction workers who were inside the work van Salgado Araujo was driving when he was shot and killed by an ICE officer on July 7. One of the other witnesses in ICE custody is Salgado Araujo's brother.

The deadly shooting, which was followed by the fatal shooting of a Colombian immigrant at the hands of an ICE agent in Maine less than a week later, reignited the national debate over President Trump's aggressive deportation blitz.

The Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, said one of its agents shot Salgado Araujo in self-defense, claiming the Mexican immigrant weaponized his work van during a traffic stop. Salgado Araujo's family has disputed that version of events, demanding an independent investigation into the killing. While it has said that Salgado Araujo was in the U.S. illegally, DHS has admitted that ICE agents were looking for a different person when they stopped his vehicle.

Last week, the FBI submitted an affidavit in federal court disclosing photos that an agent said indicated that methamphetamine may have been inside the work van. That allegation has been disputed by Houston's top prosecutor, Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare. And Ruby Powers, an attorney representing Salgado Araujo's brother, said the material in question was likely salt used in a homemade electrolyte mix to brave the summer heat.

Teare told CBS News last week he submitted paperwork to help the three witnesses detained by ICE get legal protections known as U visas, which shield victims of crimes from deportation if they help a law enforcement investigation.

title: The deadly ICE shooting in Maine is a consequence of the agency's shoddy hiring process
authors: Anthony L. Fisher, John Pfaff, Ja’han Jones
description:
Last week, an Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer shot and killed a Colombian national, Joan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, during a traffic stop in Biddeford, Maine.
While ICE has refused to name the officer who killed Guerrero, The Associated Press has identified him as David Brouillette.
But as more details have been revealed, the core issue of the outrageous lack of vetting and proper training for ICE agents has come into greater focus.
Around the time he joined ICE, Brouillette left Ashley a voicemail telling her he thought she should have her throat cut, according to AP, which heard a recording of the voicemail.
All of which suggests that the pool of those applying to be ICE agents will include many of those who were unqualified to find or keep other law enforcement jobs.
text:
Last week, an Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer shot and killed a Colombian national, Joan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, during a traffic stop in Biddeford, Maine. While ICE has refused to name the officer who killed Guerrero, The Associated Press has identified him as David Brouillette. And in a telling departure from its usual practices, ICE did not even try to argue that Guerrero “weaponized his vehicle” (although Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin did try to use this line at first).

The Department of Homeland Security’s official explanation is only that Guerrero tried to flee and that Brouillette shot him out of a “fear for public safety,” not his own personal safety. Guerrero is at least the 11th person shot and killed by federal immigration officials since the start of President Donald Trump’s second term. The violence at car stops has become so bad that ICE, rarely one to back down from a fight, last week ordered its agents to suspend almost all car stops, although Trump personally reversed that order the next day.

But as more details have been revealed, the core issue of the outrageous lack of vetting and proper training for ICE agents has come into greater focus.

Shortly after the shooting, one of Brouillette’s ex-wives, Ashley Brouillette, came forward to talk about his history of mental illness and domestic violence, after he called her following the shooting to ask her to vouch for his character. The story that emerged is terrifying. Ashley told reporters that he had abused her (Brouillette did not respond to efforts by the AP to get his comments on this), and court records document extensive claims of violent abuse against another ex-wife and daughter.

An immediate relative said that Brouillette was diagnosed with bipolar disorder as a child, was initially rejected from the military because of his mental health issues, allegedly contemplated suicide multiple times and regularly failed to hold down other law enforcement jobs after a stint in the military (including serving in Afghanistan, which family members feared only exacerbated his mental health problems). Brouillette said in court filings that he recently suffered brain damage after getting accidentally hit in the head with a steel beam pipe during a firefighting training program. Around the time he joined ICE, Brouillette left Ashley a voicemail telling her he thought she should have her throat cut, according to AP, which heard a recording of the voicemail. Both Ashley and the other ex-wife had taken out restraining orders against him, and at least one other family member said he had cut off contact out of fear.

In fact, Ashley said that when Brouillette told her in 2025 that he had joined ICE, she assumed he was having a mental health episode and didn’t believe him, because she could not imagine that ICE would hire someone with his history. Yet ICE had in fact hired him despite all these red flags, many of them easily discoverable during a background check.

And the most likely explanation is straight-forward: one major cost of ICE’s attempted hiring surge has been an apparent breakdown in vetting.

In February, Reuters reported on an internal ICE memo saying that the surge in new hires had overwhelmed the background check process. And while ICE denied that allegation, it’s hard to reconcile that denial with evidence given in a recent report by congressional Democrats showing that over 100 officials from the Federal Emergency Management Agency were assigned to ICE — perhaps in violation of federal law — to assist with background checks. Another AP investigation found that ICE had deployed numerous new hires with problematic histories before background checks were completed, including former police officers with credible claims of abusing their authority; DHS acknowledged to the AP that some ICE agents began working on a temporary status prior to the end of their vetting.

This failure of background checks would be concerning in any context, but it is especially so here, given that there are very real concerns about the professionalism of those applying for these jobs in the first place. (ICE, for its part, maintains that the officer involved in the Biddeford shooting had a decade of federal law enforcement experience, with the use-of-force training that entails, though the agency has still not identified who that officer is.)

ICE is distinctly less popular than local police, it often pays less than many police departments (especially larger urban ones), and unlike a local police job, ICE requires deployment all across the country. All of which suggests that the pool of those applying to be ICE agents will include many of those who were unqualified to find or keep other law enforcement jobs.

More from MS NOW Daily

Must reads from Today's list

People exactly like Brouillette.

This adverse selection problem likely plagues not only ICE’s efforts to hire former law enforcement officials like Brouillette, but to hire fresh candidates as well — the process for which has already faced intense scrutiny over sub-par candidates. But here, too, ICE has chosen to exacerbate rather than address (or even just ignore) the problem.

In a desperate effort to push more candidates through the Federal Law Enforcement Training Center, in the fall of 2025, ICE cut new officer training from 72 days to just 42, for a total training time of about 360 hours. Even before the cuts, the training time was well below the average for U.S. police (over 100 days, and somewhere between 650 to 850 hours), and stunningly below the time many European countries require, which range from about 2,000 to 5,500 hours.

While ICE asserted that it made no cuts to its training, and that the training it provides is sufficient, it’s still the case that ICE agents train for about two to four months, compared to 2 1/2 to 3 1/2 years for German police..

ICE did revert in July to its original 72-day program. But hundreds of agents who graduated under the shorter program are likely now out in the field, and even the 72-day program remains low by U.S. standards despite ICE recruits likely being weaker and riskier than the average police trainee.

Compounding all these problems, too, is that these higher-risk, poorly trained officers are then being deployed by an agency that appears to operate with near-impunity. While Vice President JD Vance was incorrect when he said that ICE officers have “absolute immunity” from prosecution, the reality is that the FBI regularly stonewalls local officials trying to to investigate cases of lethal ICE violence. The Department of Justice has likewise dragged its feet in assisting local officials investigating ICE and Border Patrol shootings (who are pressing charges in no small part because the DOJ won’t), and the Supreme Court has made it close to impossible to sue such officers for violating people’s rights.

Poorly trained, poorly vetted, subjected to almost no meaningful oversight. The rash of recent ICE shootings shows where that administrative strategy has taken us.

text:
A Mexican national killed in Florida while running from Immigration and Customs Enforcement was a tourist with a valid visa, according to several reports.

Juan Jairo Coronilla Durán, a 28-year-old from the Mexican state of Guanajuato, has been identified as the man fatally hit by a tractor-trailer in St. Augustine last Tuesday.

The New York Times and the Miami Herald published the man’s identity, along with other details about his trip, given to them by the Orlando-based farmworker non-profit Colectivo Árbol, which is hosting Coronilla Durán’s wife, Jessica Alamilla.

A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security told The Independent that its officers conducted an operation near St. Johns, Florida, about a 30-minute drive northwest of St Augustine, last Tuesday.

Without providing details about the encounter, the spokesperson said Florida Highway Patrol and Homeland Security Investigations have launched a probe into “an incident resulting in the death of a Mexican national.”

“We will provide an update when available,” the spokesperson added, without naming the person.

According to Coronilla Durán’s wife, he was in the U.S. on a valid tourist visa for three weeks with friends, first visiting Georgia, then Florida, Isaret Jeffers, a spokesperson for Colectivo Árbol, said.

“He was going to return this past Saturday. He had already bought a flight,” Jeffers told the Herald. “Now, unfortunately, if he is returning, his return is different.”

Coronilla Durán was trying to flee an encounter with agents from ICE and Homeland Security Investigations at a Wawa gas station when he ran into a busy road and was struck by the truck, according to the Times.

Truck driver Jose Rivera, who witnessed the incident, told the Herald that when Coronilla Durán reached the median of the road, he slipped and fell. He then picked himself up but stumbled onto the other lane of traffic, according to Rivera.

“The traffic was coming pretty quick, and he just lost his footing and didn’t look where the traffic was coming,” Rivera said.

Coronilla Durán was a father of two who had been married to Alamilla for a decade. Alamilla arrived in the U.S. last Friday to claim her husband’s body, according to Jeffers.

Coronilla Durán owned a restaurant in San Luis de La Paz, Jeffers said, telling the Times, “He didn’t want to stay in the United States.”

The Independent has reached out to Florida’s Department of Highway Safety and Motor Vehicles for comment.

Coronilla Durán’s death comes after ICE agents fatally shot a 52-year-old Mexican man, Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, in Houston and a 25-year-old Colombian native, Joan Sebastian Guerrero, in Maine at traffic stops on July 7 and 13, respectively.

The Homeland Security Department said an ICE officer fired his weapon at Guerrero because he feared for “public safety,” and Salgado Araujo was shot in “self-defense.”

title: In Ohio case, federal judge says warrantless ICE arrests are illegal, but denies motion to stop them
description:

One federal official “testified that almost all of his agency’s arrests are warrantless,” the judge’s order said.
They asked Morrison to certify the case as a class action and order the government to stop making improper warrantless arrests.

text:
A federal judge sitting in Cincinnati, Ohio on Friday ruled that federal authorities are making illegal immigration arrests. Then she dismissed a case seeking to stop the practice.

U.S. District Judge Sarah D. Morrison, a 2018 Trump appointee, ruled that Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents had made many arrests in Ohio that “deeply trouble the Court.” They were illegal, she said, because they were made without a warrant and without making a determination that a person would flee before a warrant could be obtained.

One federal official “testified that almost all of his agency’s arrests are warrantless,” the judge’s order said.

Then she dismissed the case because she said the plaintiffs didn’t do an adequate job of showing the Trump administration is likely to keep making such arrests. She made the ruling even as ICE insists it doesn’t need warrants.

Groups defending the immigrants who brought the case were not pleased.

“The opinion from the court confirms what we already knew: ICE violated the law and arrested our clients illegally,” said Angela Plummer, executive director of Community and Refugee Immigration Services, one of the groups representing the plaintiffs.

“Unfortunately, we are living in a world where documented human rights violations alone are insufficient to compel court action to stop them.”

The case was brought in March by four people who argued warrantless immigration arrests were so common that the case should be a class action and include all similarly situated people.

As the Trump administration tries to arrest 3,000 immigrants a day, critics say it’s run roughshod over due process, sweeping up people who are here legally and even some citizens.

In her ruling, Judge Morrison agreed with the plaintiffs that before making arrests, ICE agents need to have both probable cause to believe a person is in violation of immigration law and is likely to flee before a warrant can be obtained.

“Upon a fulsome review of the record in this case, it is clear that (ICE agents) have, in some instances, unlawfully arrested and detained non-citizens in Ohio without a warrant and without a probable cause determination of their likelihood of escape,” Morrison’s ruling said. “Some of the accounts offered by Plaintiffs and (the class) they wish to represent about how individual agents effectuated arrests deeply trouble the Court.”

One of the plaintiffs in the case was Moises Javier Aguilar Peralta, 38, who came to Ohio from Honduras in 2023, sought asylum and got a work permit, Social Security number, and a driver’s license.

On Dec. 18, as he walked out of a Columbus Home Depot with materials he needed for work, four masked men in civilian clothes stopped him. When he told them he had an active asylum case, the agents told him it wasn’t valid and arrested him, the suit said.

They didn’t ask him any questions to determine the legality of his presence in the country or to determine if he was a flight risk, it said.

As with the other plaintiffs, Peralta was held — and unable to support his family — for weeks and lived in a state of terror after his release, his lawyers said.

As of late March, around 670 immigrants in Ohio were in ICE detention.

“Countless of these individuals were arrested and detained without a warrant and without any pre-arrest, individualized determination of probable cause,” the plaintiffs said.

They asked Morrison to certify the case as a class action and order the government to stop making improper warrantless arrests.

Judge Morrison rejected the request, saying the four original plaintiffs didn’t adequately show they were likely to be re-arrested. But if the class were certified, re-arrests among that much-larger group would have been much more likely.

Morrison acknowledged the pressure Trump is putting on ICE to make thousands of arrests a day. She also heard from U.S. Border Patrol Acting Deputy Patrol Agent in Charge Steven Vorholt.

“Agent Vorholt, a supervisor who oversees and evaluates the field operations of USBP agents and their supervisors, testified that almost all of his agency’s arrests are warrantless,” Judge Morrison wrote.

In addition, she acknowledged that other courts have found that federal agents are making illegal, warrantless immigration arrests.

And ICE’s own website flatly says its agents don’t need warrants to arrest people they believe are in violation of immigration law.

“ICE does not need judicial warrants to make arrests,” it says. “Like all other law enforcement officers, ICE officers and agents can initiate consensual encounters and speak with people, briefly detain aliens when they have reasonable suspicion that the aliens are illegally present in the United States, and arrest people they believe are illegal aliens.”

Even so, Judge Morrison said the plaintiffs fell short because they didn’t show federal immigration arrests are always warrantless or that the agencies have a written policy to act illegally. She cited internal documents saying agents needed to get warrants in cases where escape wasn’t imminent.

“In this case, Plaintiffs have not shown that all of Defendants’ agents always make warrantless arrests without determining the non-citizen arrestee’s likelihood of escape,” she wrote.

“Nor have Plaintiffs shown that either ICE or CBP adopted a written policy of unlawful conduct. Although the Court finds that Plaintiffs have shown for jurisdictional purposes that Defendants authorized their agents, through an unofficial custom or practice, to make unlawful warrantless arrests in Ohio, Plaintiffs have not convinced the Court that Defendants are sufficiently likely to subject them to another arrest under that practice.”

Freda Levinson, the chief legal officer of ACLU of Ohio, found a partial victory in the ruling.

“This ruling is deeply disappointing and frustrating, but it also recognizes that federal agents are wantonly conducting haphazard arrests in clear violation of the dictates and the Immigration and Nationality Act,” she said in a written statement.

text:
JULY 20, 2026

Contact: info@haitianbridge.org, Paige Censale, pcensale@haitianbridge.org

SAN DIEGO, CA — Haitian Bridge Alliance (HBA) condemns the Trump administration’s expansion of deportation flights to the Republic of Haiti as the country faces an unprecedented humanitarian and security crisis. Just days before more than 350,000 Haitians are set to lose work authorization under Temporary Protected Status (TPS), the administration has begun increasing removals, with U.S. officials informing Haiti that deportation flights are expected to increase to at least two per week following the expiration of TPS protections. The first expanded flight arrived in Cap-Haïtien on Thursday July 16, 2026 carrying 111 people, although the U.S. government advises Americans to not travel to Haiti due to safety concerns. Furthermore, the State Department has issued additional travel advisory asking American citizens to leave their DNA samples behind with a medical provider or dental record with family if they intend to travel to the island.

“These deportations are adding fuel to an already devastating humanitarian catastrophe. The U.S. continues to contribute to the destabilization of the country through its draconian and racist foreign policy” said Guerline Jozef, Executive Director of Haitian Bridge Alliance. “The United States is knowingly returning people to a country overwhelmed by violence, mass displacement, and institutional collapse. Rather than protecting human life, these removals will deepen instability, separate families, and place countless people in harm’s way. This is inhumane and a violation under international human rights law”

The Haitian government has warned that it lacks the capacity to absorb a significant increase in deportations, as humanitarian organizations struggle to respond to the growing needs of internally displaced persons and the thousands of Haitians already being returned from neighboring countries each month. Haiti’s Prime Minister has publicly stated that “this is not the time” to return Haitians, citing the country’s worsening security and humanitarian conditions.

“Haiti cannot safely receive large numbers of deportees while communities are under siege and nearly 1.5 million people have already been forced from their homes,” Jozef added. “The United States should be extending protection—not accelerating deportations into one of the world’s most dangerous humanitarian crises.”

Haitian Bridge Alliance calls on the Administration and Congress to:

Immediately suspend all deportations to Haiti.

Restore and extend Temporary Protected Status for Haitian nationals.

Expand humanitarian protections for Haitians fleeing violence and persecution.

Ensure U.S. immigration policy reflects the reality of Haiti’s ongoing humanitarian emergency.

Pass S. 4814, A bill to require the Secretary of Homeland Security to designate Haiti for temporary protected status for three years.

Pass comprehensive immigration reform to create a pathway to green card and U.S. citizenship for all TPS holders.

Haiti is experiencing a humanitarian crisis. Despite this, Temporary Protected Status(TPS)for Haitian nationals is set toterminateas early as July 24, 2026. Byadvancing S.4814, Members of the Senate can help protect Haitians from being forcibly returned to life-threatening conditions. Senators should also urge the President togrant Deferred Enforced Departure (DED)to Haitian nationals until legislation is passed.

Take Action

What is happening in Haiti?

Haiti was first designated for TPS in 2010 after catastrophic earthquakes. Over the last decade, its designation has continued to be extended, and even renewed through redesignations several times, due to ongoing violence, displacement, and political instability. Human rights organizations report widespread insecurity and the government’s failure to protect civilians.

What is Temporary Protected Status?

Temporary Protected Status (TPS) is a humanitarian protection under U.S. law that allows people from designated countries to remain temporarily in the United States when conditions in their home country prevent safe return.

TPS may be designated when a country is experiencing:

Ongoing armed conflict

Environmental disaster

Extraordinary and temporary conditions that make return unsafe

While TPS does not provide permanent immigration status, it does offer temporary protection from deportation and allows recipients to work legally while in this status.

For an estimated 330,000 Haitian nationals living in the United States, TPS provides critical stability for families, workers, and others who cannot safely return home. Additionally, TPS holders provide stability to domestic industries that face staffing shortages. For example, more than 112,000 Haitians work in the U.S. healthcare industry.

Why is this issue urgent now?

The need for action is urgent because protection for Haitian nationals is set to terminate as early as July 24, 2026.

Late last year, former DHS Secretary Kristi Noem announced termination of Haiti’s Temporary Protected Status (TPS) designation, despite the ongoing humanitarian crisis there. While this termination was paused during court battles, the Supreme Court’s decision in Mullin v. Doe removed any obstacles for termination.

This decision places Haitian TPS holders at risk of imminent deportation. Without protection, they face return to a country marked by conflict, violence, and political instability.

What impact does TPS termination have on Americans?

According to the American Immigration Council, over 112,800 Haitians work in the U.S. healthcare industry alone. All TPS holders may work legally. They serve as nurses, home health aides for the elderly, and caregivers in long-term facilities. The Supreme Court’s ruling brings uncertainty and fear not only for these workers, but also for the thousands of vulnerable American patients who rely on them.

The U.S. is experiencing its fastest increase in the ageing population in more than 100 years, but the number of caregivers has not matched the growth. In January 2026, nearly 15,000 nurses in New York went on strike to protest unsafe staffing ratios. A recent study indicates that a third of all hospitals face nursing vacancies of 10% or more. In a healthcare system already facing staffing shortages, removing a significant percentage of eligible workers will further endanger patients.

Why the Senate should act

The House took the first steps, passing H.R. 1689. This bipartisan effort directs the Department of Homeland Security to extend Haiti’s TPS until 2029. Senators Edward J. Markey (D-Mass.) and Lisa Blunt Rochester (D-Del.) have now introduced companion legislation (S.4814).

The Senate should act because there is a clear and imminent humanitarian need. The consequences of inaction would be severe.

As Bishop Brendan J. Cahill, chairman of the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops’ (USCCB) wrote, “Revoking the legal status of hundreds of thousands of people residing in our country creates a moral crisis when returning to their country of origin is not a safe or reasonable option.”

text:
An examination of cases in which people were arrested for supposedly assaulting an immigration agent finds that nearly half of those charges were either dropped or resulted in no conviction — suggesting that federal law enforcement has engaged in widespread misconduct in carrying out President Donald Trump’s mass deportation campaign.

The New York Times report, published on July 18, examined the close to 550 cases in which individuals — generally protesters and/or immigrants — were arrested for assault due to their alleged conduct during interactions with immigration agents since President Donald Trump returned to office. Of those arrests, 459 cases have been resolved so far.

Of those, 246 cases ended in a guilty plea from those who were charged. Only four cases that went to trial resulted in a conviction.

Conversely, 213 of the total assault cases observed resulted in jury acquittals, judges tossing out the charges, or prosecutors withdrawing the case.

The DOJ is accustomed to a higher success rate, with around 90 percent of people who face charges from the department typically either being found guilty or making a guilty plea arrangement.

“There seems to be a pattern of charges being filed without any merit,” former Chicago-based federal prosecutor Jimmy Arce told the Times.

The report comes as federal immigration agencies, such as Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), are facing renewed scrutiny for their violent tactics in cities across the U.S.

Last week, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) temporarily suspended ICE agents from engaging in traffic stops after agents shot and killed two men, one from Maine and the other from Texas. Neither individual was engaged in illegal actions at the time of their stop.

After that enforcement action was halted, President Donald Trump intervened, demanding on Truth Social that the pause be lifted.

“We CANNOT give up one of ICE’s most important and effective Crime Fighting tools, THE TRAFFIC STOP! Once we do, we are playing right into the criminal’s hands,” Trump wrote.

In the wake of these killings, new polling reveals that most Americans are deeply distrustful of ICE.

According to an Economist/YouGov poll published on Tuesday, only 38 percent of voters say they have “a great deal” of or “some” confidence in the agency. Meanwhile, 53 percent said they have “only a little” or no confidence “at all” in ICE.

A plurality of respondents, 48 percent, said they’d like to see the agency abolished, with 40 percent disagreeing.

Trump himself has seen his polling numbers on immigration slip dramatically. Once a strong issue for the president, only 39 percent now approve of how he’s handling immigration, according to the poll, while 54 percent disapprove.

text:
Members of the House Foreign Affairs committee challenged the Trump administration Tuesday over what Democrats described as a contradiction in U.S. policy: ending deportations protections for hundreds of thousands of Haitians living in the United States while simultaneously spending millions of dollars to support a new gang-fighting force in the Caribbean country.

“Even as the administration warns Americans against traveling to Haiti, it claims the island is safe enough to end Temporary Protected Status and deport some 350,000 Haitians,” New York Rep. Gregory Meeks, the ranking Democrat on the committee, said. “This is not just cruel; it’s contradictory, and it will only exacerbate instability in Haiti.”

Meeks’ criticism came during a hearing with Michael Kozak, the State Department’s senior official in the Bureau of Western Hemisphere Affairs, and Col. Justin Gorkowski, one of the leaders of the Tiger Team of the Gang Suppression Force’s Tiger Team at the Defense Department. While both focused opening statements on American efforts to help Haiti curb escalating gang violence through the new United Nations-authorized gang-fighting force, lawmakers repeatedly shifted the focus to the Trump administration’s decision to terminate Temporary Protected Status for Haitians.

“There’s a contradiction,” Rep. Bill Keating, a Massachusetts Democrat, said as he questioned Kozak. “It’s not safe. We have a task force, a Gang Suppression Force there, and these people were given status because of that danger. Now, it’s all of a sudden safe to send them back. Can you explain that contradiction? It’s an obvious contradiction.”

Kozak said he did not view the situation as contradictory, arguing that while he didn’t know the exact figures for Haiti, when he looks “at TPS beneficiaries in other countries, usually one thing you’ll find is that a great deal of that total number are people who’ve already adjusted status and have [legal permanent resident] status in the United States. So they probably won’t be going back.”

That assertion conflicts with how the program works. Created in 1990 by Congress, TPS allows citizens of countries affected by natural disasters, armed conflict or other extraordinary conditions to live and work temporarily in the United States, but it does not provide a legal path to permanent residency or citizenship.

Maryland Democrat Rep. Kweisi Mfume challenged Kozak’s effort to minimize the impact of ending TPS, which ends on Friday.

The president and the Department of Homeland Security have said they’re planning to round up Haitians who no longer have TPS and sending them back to Haiti, Mfume said after schooling colleagues on Haiti’s history of tyrannical rulers and failed U.S. policies over two centuries. “It is going to be a massive effort to deport all 350,000.”

“I know that ripping Haitians from their jobs and citizens’ kids that’ll be the administration’s priority,” Mfume added. “That’s an unacceptable situation, and it’s one that we should not accept.”

Supreme Court ruling

The Supreme Court last month cleared the way for DHS to end TPS protection against deportations for Haitians, ruling 6-3 that the decision by Kristi Noem, secretary of Homeland Security Secretary at the time, is not subject to judicial review. The administration had appealed two lower court rulings that blocked the termination.

Twice during Tuesday’s hearing lawmakers asked Kozak whether the State Department had been consulted before Noem ended Haiti’s TPS designation, as required by statute.

“I don’t believe so,” he said.

He argued not all of Haiti was under gang control and quoted Prime Minister Alix Didier Fils-Aimé as saying seven of the country’s 10 regional departments could hold elections “tomorrow.”

“They’re stable and life goes on as normal,” Kozak said. “It’s Port-au-Prince and Artibonite and the West that are the problem.”

U.N. officials have warned that armed groups now control large swaths of the West, which includes Port-au-Prince, and are expanding their territory. Gang violence has spread into southeastern Haiti, while there were mass killings in the hills above Port-au-Prince earlier his month. Children, meanwhile, account for nearly half of all gang recruits, according to the U.N.

Republicans defended the administration’s approach while arguing that U.S. taxpayers have shouldered too much of Haiti’s security crisis.

“The administration has rolled out bilateral assistance piece by piece, up to $40 million in bridge and sustainment funds, $68 million in equipment, a police recruitment surge, support for Haiti’s armed forces, and now counterterrorism funds, with no specific dollar figure attached,” Florida Republican Rep. Brian Mast said. “That money, by the State Department’s own accounting, is going toward, among other things, buying meals ready to eat and bottled water. A bill that the department itself says belongs to those countries.”

Mast, the committee chairman, said the purpose of the hearing was to examine the U.S. response to the security crisis and the gang-fighting force after what he and others called the failure of an earlier effort by the Kenya-led Multinational Security Support mission.

“I’d like to see the ledger of what Kenya grifted off of the United States of America for this, off the American taxpayer,” Mast said.

In his opening remarks, Mast noted that Haiti lies 700 miles from Florida and terrorist organizations effectively control the capital.

“They hold an estimated 90% of Port-au-Prince. They have displaced more than 1.4 million,” he said. “They murder, they kidnap, they rape, they castrate, they feed people what they castrate.

“They extort the Haitian people on a massive scale. They seek to replace the Haitian state with something that answers to them. The consequences of a fully collapsed Haiti will not just stay in Haiti,” Mast added. “It goes without saying that mass illegal immigration from a country explicitly governed as a safe haven for terrorists and traffickers would be harmful to America’s interests, those of our allies.”

Pennsylvania Republican Rep. Scott Perry said it would seem that his Democratic colleagues “would export all 12 million Haitians to America because it’s so dangerous there.

“If every good person in Haiti that’s not involved in organized crime, gang activity…leaves Haiti, how is Haiti ever going to get better? Somebody has to love Haiti and want to save Haiti,” he said.

Perry noted that the U.S. has provided more than $5.1 billion in assistance to Haiti since a massive earthquake in 2010 and that international donors pledged more than $13 billion. Much of that promised aid, however, was never delivered. Meanwhile, Canaan, a massive settlement created after the earthquake under U.S. pressure, has today become one of the country’s largest gang strongholds.

Members of Congress also tried but failed to get answers to growing concerns over the use of American-linked private military contractors in Haiti’s anti-gang campaign. A Human Rights Watch report has said drone strikes in Haiti carried out by private contractors working for Vectus Global and Haitian security forces have killed at least 1,243 people, including 17 children.

“We cannot confirm or deny whether any particular license has been issued to any company or not,” Kozak said when asked for details about the firm’s dealings. The firm is owned by Erik Prince, the former U.S. Navy SEAL officer who founded the private military contractor Blackwater.

“Haiti’s very important, especially to us in the great state of Florida. But it’s significantly important to me as the only member of Congress who went and traveled over to Haiti in April of 2024 and conducted rescues,” Florida Republican Rep. Cory Mills said.

During one mission, he said he rescued 59 mentally and physically disabled children who had been targeted by gang leaders who “would take their food and their medicine to watch them slowly die,” Mills said.

“This is the type of barbarism that we can’t accept, especially this close to our own shorelines,” he said. “We need Congress to have better reporting and briefings, and we need to have the information so that we can use tools.”

‘Proto-insurgency’

Despite their disagreements over TPS, lawmakers from both parties appeared to agree on the scale of Haiti’s security crisis.

“The absence of governance in Haiti has created opportunities for informed power structures to thrive through use of force, financial independence, intimidation and terrorism. Over 20 different gang leaders deploy their foot soldiers to fight for control over Haiti’s territory and dwindling resources,” Gorkowski said in his opening. “These are not simple gangs that can be jailed and prosecuted.”

Previous international efforts, including the Kenya-led force, had mischaracterized the conflict, he argued.

“They thought of this as a criminal problem. It is not,” said Gorkowski, who helped design the new gang-fighting response. “This is a proto-insurgency, and these folks really are on the verge of something significant.”

Haiti’s security forces number only a fraction of what is needed, he said, estimating the country requires 30,000 security personnel to restore order. Until then, he argued, Haiti will remain dependent on the Gang Suppression Force and international support.

Defeating the gangs, Gorkowski said, require four elements to be dismantled: “Arms and ammunition, illicit revenue generation, safe havens and alliance.”

Failing to do this, Kozak said, means allowing gangs to basically take over a failed state, “operating, running drugs, running human trafficking, exporting all manner of chaos in the region and directly to the United States, and a huge, massive outflow of additional people who would be fleeing that chaos. So that that’s what we don’t want.”

text:
WASHINGTON — Dozens of Democratic U.S. senators and the Independent senator from Maine pushed for more details Monday from Immigration and Customs Enforcement about the agency’s vetting practices for new agents and how officers conduct vehicle pursuits, even as they demanded that body cameras be swiftly rolled out to all officers.

The demands came in a letter spearheaded by Maine’s Independent Sen. Angus King, signed by 38 Democratic senators and sent to the Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE. The demands follow two deadly shootings in which ICE officers shot and killed immigrants in Houston and Maine.

The Associated Press reported last week that the ICE officer in Maine who opened fire and killed a man from Colombia had a history of violent behavior toward family members that was detailed in family court records.

His first ex-wife, Ashley Brouillette, told AP he was physically violent with her, including once throwing boiling water at her while she was holding their child.

His second ex-wife, Lucinda Brouillette, sent a statement over the weekend alleging "a persistent pattern of abuse, intimidation, manipulation, fear, and control."

"Throughout our marriage and in the years that followed, I have feared for a long time that his anger, aggression, and escalating behavior would eventually result in severe, life threatening violence, and I often believed I would be the one on the receiving end of it," she wrote.

Hundreds of pages of family court documents describe their turbulent marriage, and the years after. Lucinda Brouillette told the court he had stalked and harassed her and physically and verbally abused his daughter, according to multiple requests for temporary protection orders. Brouillette tackled his teenage daughter and smashed spaghetti in her hair, and during another outburst, he dragged his daughter around the house as she cried, she said.

"Dave needs counseling or something for his PTSD & depression," she wrote in an application for a temporary protective order on behalf of his teenage daughter which a judge granted in 2021.

In court filings, David Brouillette said that his second ex-wife had slandered him.

Multiple family members told the AP the government should have never given him a gun, badge and the authority to patrol city streets as the Trump administration ramps up its mass deportation agenda.

The senators’ letter on Monday listed new measures to increase accountability at the agency, including transparency about whether ICE considers records from family court of domestic violence or abuse when vetting new recruits.

“We remain supportive of removing dangerous convicted criminals from our communities, but this goal can and must be achieved without endangering these very communities in the process. By no stretch could either of the victims in Texas and Maine be characterized as ‘the worst of the worst,' making these tragic deaths even more egregious,” the senators wrote. "The American people deserve clarity and accountability."

They said ICE should immediately start wearing uniforms or vests that clearly identify them as "ICE" instead of the more generic "POLICE" or "POLICE ICE." Civil rights groups and advocates have often criticized ICE for not wearing uniforms or clear identification on their ballistics vests identifying them as deportation officers.

Senators also demanded to know what changes were being made to how officers conduct traffic stops and vehicle pursuits.

The shootings in Maine and Houston both involved ICE officers shooting at people who were in vehicles at the time. In the wake of the Maine shooting, Homeland Security temporarily stopped officers from conducting vehicle stops except in specific situations. But just a day later, after fierce criticism from some MAGA supporters, President Donald Trump said on social media that traffic stops should continue.

text:
A Mexican man who was struck and killed by a tractor trailer in Florida after running from federal immigration officers was vacationing in the U.S. and had a tourist visa, according to a Mexico official and a group assisting his wife.

Juan Jairo Coronilla Durán, 28, died July 14 after authorities said he darted across a busy road in St. Augustine and into the path of a truck. His death was the third in roughly a week involving encounters with Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents, following fatal shootings in Texas and Maine.

Coronilla Durán traveled from his hometown of San Luis de la Paz, in the central Mexican state of Guanajuato, to Atlanta to visit family and friends, according to Isaret Jeffers, founder of Colectivo Arbol, a farmworkers advocacy group. He had stayed in Georgia for three weeks before traveling to Florida's east coast to enjoy the beaches, Jeffers said Tuesday.

U.S. authorities have not publicly identified the man, but a Mexico official confirmed his name. Jeffers said Yezzika Alamilla, the man's wife, told them he had been visiting the U.S. on a tourist visa.

The Department of Homeland Security did not immediately respond to an email seeking comment Tuesday about whether Coronilla Durán had a valid visa.

Coronilla Durán was one of four people in a vehicle that stopped in a gas station parking lot before 7 a.m. on the day he died. The four fled on foot during an encounter with agents from U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Homeland Security Investigations, with one darting across a busy road into the path of the semi, the Florida Highway Patrol said.

It is unclear what prompted the encounter and what happened to the vehicle's other three occupants.

The Highway Patrol and DHS have not provided additional details, citing the ongoing investigation.

Alamilla called Colectivo Arbol, which provides legal advice and assistance to farmworkers in Central Florida, the day after her husband died, Jeffers said. She was seeking help to travel from Mexico and repatriate her husband's remains. The organization bought her a plane ticket and put her up for three days, until Monday, she said. The Mexican consulate has been helping her since.

"His wife said he was there on a tourist visa. She didn't understand what was happening," Jeffers said. "He didn't come to work; he wasn't working. He was here as a tourist."

Alamilla "thinks he was very afraid, and that's why he ran away," Jeffers said.

According to information provided by the widow, Coronilla Durán "had been in the United States for only a very short time (and) had a tourist visa," said Susana Guerra Vallejo, the undersecretary for assistance to migrants and mobility issues for the Mexican state of Guanajuato.

She said that Alamilla would be able to see the body of her husband at the Florida funeral home.

Coronilla Durán's body will be transported to Mexico on a commercial flight from Orlando, Guerra Vallejo told The Associated Press. He will be buried in his hometown of San Luis de la Paz, a farming community in Guanajuato that is about 160 miles northwest of Mexico City, she said.

Coronilla Durán and Alamilla had two children, a 7-month-old girl and a 7-year-old boy, Jeffers said.

Coronilla Durán's death was at least the 10th involving encounters with immigration agents since President Trump launched his mass deportation campaign last year.

His death came one day after an ICE officer shot and killed a Colombian man in Biddeford, Maine. Just days earlier, on July 7, an ICE officer shot and killed a Mexican national in Houston who had lived in the U.S. for decades.

The Mexican government said it had asked state attorneys general in the U.S. to review the deaths of migrants in ICE custody or during raids for possible criminal prosecution.
