WASHINGTON — As many as 20,000 unaccompanied immigrant children are at risk of losing their federally funded legal representation due to the Trump administration withholding appropriated funds, immigration attorneys warned Tuesday.

For more than six months, the Health and Human Services Department’s Office of Refugee Resettlement has not released $65 million Congress appropriated for legal representation of unaccompanied children in immigration cases. That means children may have to press their immigration claims on their own, vastly raising the probability they will be deported, the attorneys said.

“Children are now facing the real possibility of representing themselves alone against experienced government attorneys,” Ana Devereaux, an attorney at the Michigan Immigrant Rights Center, said during a virtual press conference.

Shaina Aber, the executive director for Acacia Center for Justice, a national group that partners with at least 100 legal organizations to provide services to children, said the lack of funding is already being felt. Several of the group’s partners have declined to continue the partnerships because they have not been reimbursed, she said.

Aber said the funds were withheld because attorneys refused to hand over to the administration sensitive case data from the unaccompanied children, such as medical records and the types of legal relief the minors are seeking.

“These children should not, and should never be, leveraged in a political game,” she said.

HHS did not respond to States Newsroom's request for comment.

‘Children are children’

Without a lawyer, fewer than 10% of immigrant children win the right to remain in the United States while their case goes through immigration court, said Elizabeth Young, a former immigration judge.

Some children going through the courts are too young to speak, she said during the press conference.

“A legal system that values fairness cannot expect children to carry that burden alone,” Young said.

Devereaux said the Michigan Immigrant Rights Center is operating on reserves and has continued to provide legal services for about 1,100 children.

“Children are children, regardless of their nationality,” Devereaux said.

Stripping away the legal services for children, Aber said, is “yet another system of mass deportations.”

Additionally, the Trump administration does not plan to renew its contract with Acacia, which ends July 31, Aber said.

Instead, the administration is eyeing a small Texas state commission that aids low-income people with criminal defense to provide legal services for immigrant children. The commission does not have experience handling immigration cases or unaccompanied minors, Aber said.

Lawmakers push to release funds

Democratic members of Congress have also called on the Trump administration to release the funds, which Congress approved.

Last month, more than 70 lawmakers demanded that ORR reimburse the legal groups.

“Ultimately, we are concerned that these payment delays may be an attempt to circumvent requirements that ORR continue funding legal services for unaccompanied children,” they wrote. “The federal government must meet its obligations under the law.”

Congress created the Unaccompanied Children Program, which, among other things, provides funding for legal representation of migrant children. Free legal representation is not generally provided for immigrants but there is a carveout for unaccompanied children.

There are about 100 organizations across the U.S. that provide those legal services.

The move from the Trump administration to withhold funds has sparked several lawsuits. Last year, a preliminary injunction was put in place that ordered the federal government to continue funding legal services for unaccompanied children.

But advocates have not received any funds since December and were back in court this month.

Last week, federal Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín of the U.S. District Court for the District of Northern California probed whether the Trump administration should be held in contempt over the withholding of funds after 11 groups claimed they have still not received any reimbursements, according to El Paso Matters.

Those groups are the Amica Center for Immigrant Rights, Community Legal Services in East Palo Alto, Estrella del Paso, Florence Immigrant & Refugee Rights Project, Galveston-Houston Immigrant Representation Project, Immigrant Defenders Law Center, National Immigrant Justice Center, Northwest Immigrant Rights Project, Rocky Mountain Immigrant Advocacy Network, Social Justice Collaborative and the Vermont Asylum Assistance Project.

text:
By Sarah Nelson

Star Tribune

MINNEAPOLIS — A federal judge on Monday dismissed a lawsuit by the Justice Department targeting Minnesota’s laws prohibiting law enforcement from assisting U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents, saying state and local laws do not intrude on federal authority.

In a 56-page order, Chief U.S. District Judge Eric Tostrud rejected the Justice Department’s claims that Minnesota’s laws unfairly target federal immigration agents and inhibit them from carrying out immigration work.

| REGISTER: Building public confidence in an era of public safety innovation

“They do not command the federal government or its contractors to act. They do not forbid the federal government or its contractors from acting. They do not control how the federal government or its contractors undertake their work. Rather, they regulate how state and local officials perform their duties,” wrote Tostrud, a President Donald Trump appointee.

The Department of Justice did not immediately respond to the Minnesota Star Tribune’s request for comment about the order.

Filed in September, the lawsuit preceded Operation Metro Surge — the immigration crackdown in Minnesota that sent roughly 4,000 agents to the state. The administration asked the court to declare Minnesota’s policies unconstitutional and prohibit the state from enforcing them. In addition to suing the state, the Trump administration also sued Minneapolis, St. Paul and Hennepin County over ordinances that limited assistance with immigration enforcement.

The targeted policies included a prohibition on sharing driver’s license information with federal immigration agents and ordinances limiting what local police can share with federal immigration officers. Lawyers for the state and cities argued they should not be responsible for enforcing civil immigration law.

“Minnesota is not impeding immigration law, it is just not assisting,” wrote attorneys for the state in response to the lawsuit.

In his order, Tostrud said forcing Minnesota or cities to assist with civil federal immigration policies would violate the anticommandeering doctrine under the 10th Amendment, which prevents the federal government from compelling states to carry out its orders. He determined that forcing states to assist in federal immigration matters may cause the state budgetary concerns by shifting resources toward enforcing federal law.

He also rejected the federal government’s claims that Minnesota’s immigration laws single out the federal government, saying Minnesota laws also extend to private companies and state governments.

In a statement, Attorney General Keith Ellison praised the ruling and said Tostrud’s order “reaffirmed longstanding principle that the federal government cannot force Minnesota or any state to participate in its misguided immigration-enforcement efforts or commandeer state resources for it.”

“The Trump Administration , however, has no regard for this constitutional principle, so it nonetheless filed this lawsuit as part of its ongoing war against the people of Minnesota and its efforts to intimidate us into submission,” Ellison’s statement said. “They keep learning over and over that the people of Minnesota won’t be intimidated. Nor will I.”

The Trump administration has continued to make immigration a cornerstone of the president’s second term and target jurisdictions that have so-called “sanctuary” policies.

Last week, Maryland was among the latest to face a a Justice Department lawsuit over its laws. Some federal courts across the U.S. have dismissed similar lawsuits brought by the Justice Department , including in Los Angeles, Illinois, New Jersey and New York.

The suit against Minnesota came after Trump issued an executive order to identify jurisdictions that defy federal immigration law. Minnesota was later listed among a dozen states by the Justice Department for being a “sanctuary jurisdiction.”

title: Trump's Debanking Plan Will Boost Self-Deportations | FAIRUS.org
description:
By directing regulators to treat lack of legal work authorization as a serious credit risk, the new debanking policy has the potential to be a self-deportation engine.
This, in tandem with physical barriers, E-Verify expansion, and workplace enforcement, represents the smartest remedies for illegal mass migration in generations.
Mass illegal migration cannot be solved by border enforcement alone.
The United States has both the right and the responsibility to decide who may participate fully in its economy.
The Trump administration’s debanking guidance is a practical innovation that strengthens deterrence, encourages self-deportation, protects American workers and taxpayers, and reinforces the rule of law.
text:
When asked after his capture in 1952 why he robbed banks, the notorious Willie Sutton is alleged to have said “that’s where the money is.” Despite voluminous research and analysis of America’s problems with illegal migration, Sutton’s famous quote is the best explanation why foreign nationals still try to break into the United States.

The magnet that lures noncitizens to break our immigration laws isn’t just jobs, but also access to direct deposit, credit cards, and a bank account. The Trump administration’s May 2026 executive order drew a roadmap to restrict that system, and now it is being implemented. That’s good news for those weary of an immigration system that looks the other way at rampant lawlessness while ignoring policies that result in greater self-deportation.

By directing regulators to treat lack of legal work authorization as a serious credit risk, the new debanking policy has the potential to be a self-deportation engine. It is low-cost and ruthlessly effective at drying up the shadow economy that attracts a seemingly infinite supply of border crossers.

The rush of foreign national to cross our borders illegally is not primarily a humanitarian crisis at the border, but an economic phenomenon driven by jobs, wages, housing, and financial services inside the United States. Migrants come because employers can hire them, pay them, and integrate them into the economy. Access to bank accounts, direct deposit, credit cards, auto loans, and mortgages allow people here illegally to live better than they did in their homelands and to send remittances home. Remove or sharply restrict that access, and the decision to come here illegally is not the no-brainer it has been until now.

The policy works through straightforward risk management already embedded in existing law. Under guidance from the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau and banking regulators, lenders must assess a borrower’s ability to repay. When repayment depends on employment that can legally end at any moment through deportation or employer compliance with immigration law, that risk rises.

Banks have every incentive to avoid losses. The administration has simply clarified that immigration status and work authorization are relevant data points in that analysis. This is not a blanket prohibition. It is targeted scrutiny that ties private-sector incentives with national interest.

This strategy is practical because it leverages institutions that already exist and operate at scale. Banks already flag suspicious activity for anti-money laundering purposes. Adding immigration-related risk factors requires no new federal bureaucracy or army of agents.

Physical removals are also expensive and require significant human resources. Self-deportation through economic pressure is cheaper and faster.

For those who claim to generally support deportations but get the ick from watching how ICE does it, the debanking plan achieves the same goals without the sometimes violent altercations. Physical removals are also expensive and require significant human resources. Self-deportation through economic pressure is cheaper and faster. More than 2 million illegal aliens have self-deported in the second Trump administration. Imagine how many more will opt out when privileges like banking, credit, and stable payroll become unreliable.

The strategy also deters future illegal entries. Potential migrants must weigh the border crossing risks, employment prospects, and long-term viability. If the message is clear that the United States will no longer provide easy financial access in an increasingly cashless society for those here illegally, fewer will make the journey. This, in tandem with physical barriers, E-Verify expansion, and workplace enforcement, represents the smartest remedies for illegal mass migration in generations.

Critics may claim this directive burdens families or disrupts communities. The reality is that being in America illegally itself creates those burdens via overcrowded schools, hospitals, and housing markets, as well as wage competition for lower-skilled American workers. The policy does not target legal immigrants or citizens. It focuses solely on individuals who entered or remained in violation of U.S. law. The result will be safer, less crowded and more prosperous communities for those with the legal right to be here.

Mass illegal migration cannot be solved by border enforcement alone. Pull factors in the interior of the country must be addressed. Jobs are the primary magnet, and access to banking and credit sustains that magnet. Cutting off or complicating that access is a direct response that requires neither new statutes nor unlimited enforcement budgets. It turns the financial sector’s natural caution into an ally of immigration enforcement.

The United States has both the right and the responsibility to decide who may participate fully in its economy. The Trump administration’s debanking guidance is a practical innovation that strengthens deterrence, encourages self-deportation, protects American workers and taxpayers, and reinforces the rule of law. Other tools remain necessary, but this one deserves recognition as an efficient force multiplier in the effort to end the era of unchecked illegal mass migration.

text:
CLIFTON PARK — Nothing is taking Johan Sandoval’s eyes off the ball — not 13 days in a federal detention center, an ankle monitor, nor a potentially lengthy legal process to correct an error in paperwork that upended his immigration status.

“They will not kill my dream,” the standout student-athlete from Savannah State University told the Times Union following his recent release from an immigration detention center near Buffalo. “My professional dream is to play baseball. Even if I don’t play in America, I will find a way. It’s been my dream for a long time.”

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Sandoval, a 22-year-old from the Dominican Republic, whom his attorney said has no criminal record, was arrested by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents on July 3 at an apartment he was staying at with his fiancée and her mother in Clifton Park. ICE officials said he was detained after agents found that a form he used to obtain a student visa expired in April 2025. He was released from federal custody on Wednesday on a $20,000 bond and ordered to wear an ankle monitor so ICE could track his movements.

An attorney for Sandoval has argued that the lapse was not his client’s fault and that the paperwork error likely happened when school officials did not update his transfer status after he left Bryant & Stratton College in 2024. He had departed for school at Savannah State in Georgia.

Sandoval said he will do what it takes to satisfy the orders from the immigration judge presiding over his case so that he can return to school and the sport he has loved since age 3. But he knows it’s not going to be easy.

On Friday, he still expressed shock over the whole ordeal: being blocked by federal agents while exiting the Clifton Park apartment complex, the act of being handcuffed and arrested, then locked up for nearly two weeks in the Buffalo Federal Detention Facility in Batavia.

“When I first got arrested, I thought, ‘Why am I here?’” he said. “I do nothing wrong. I’m a good student. I’m a good athlete. I do community service. It was really bad.”

His first stop after his arrest was at the ICE field office in Malta, where he was processed. Later that day, he was transferred to Batavia. He said he was placed in a large room with several other detainees, where he lay on the floor for two days without sleeping because there were no available beds in the unit.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

“It was a nightmare,” he recalled. “I kept trying to realize what was going on and ask God to guide me. I know how strong He is and I just kept praying for my family because I knew this was hard on my mom and dad.”

He went two days without contact with the outside world, until he was given a PIN code for the phone and a commissary at the site. He was placed in a unit he said was designated for people without criminal records.

“I had a hard battle in my mind,” Sandoval said. “The first week, I started losing hope. (Being detained was) killing my hopes. I felt no one here is going to help you. I didn’t know what time it was, what day it was. But God is great. He was always with me.”

Advertisement

Once in his unit, things somewhat improved. He met people from the Caribbean and other Latin American countries. “We have a lot in common,” he noted.

He said they gathered for Bible studies and played baseball in a recreation area. They used their sandals for bases, their hands as bats, and a small ball the detention center provided to detainees. He said he also spent time doing pull-ups and sprinting short distances in the unit.

Since childhood, Sandoval prided himself on doing the right thing by his parents — focusing on school while pursuing his passion for baseball. Going to college in America seemed like the perfect plan.

He transferred to Savannah State University after obtaining an associate degree at Bryant & Stratton. As a Tiger, he became one of the college’s top players, starting every game as a second baseman with a strong batting average. At the end of the spring season, he was named to the ABCA/Rawlings NCAA Division II All-South Region Second Team.

Article continues below this ad

He met his fiancée, Adriana Wade, while he was in school in Albany. He was spending the summer with Wade and her mother, Lynn Tiberio, when ICE arrested him at their apartment complex.

When the Times Union reached out to ICE earlier this month to ask about Sandoval’s arrest, a spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security said he tried to evade agents, but the agency did not immediately respond to a follow-up request asking for evidence of that. Tiberio disputes that Sandoval tried to run away. She said during the incident, she told Sandoval to wait on the balcony while she spoke with officers. When he came back inside, she said, he fully cooperated with offering his paperwork and when they subsequently took him into custody.

Sandoval’s attorney, John Jeha, said he is unsure why ICE is saying his client tried to flee. He also said it appeared that the immigration form the school fills out to certify the student’s eligibility for enrollment was changed after Sandoval graduated from Bryant & Stratton. It was coded in a database to “terminate” instead of “transfer.”

On Monday, another attorney for Sandoval, L.J. D’Arrigo, said Sandoval’s transfer was therefore never initiated with Savannah State.

The system also never alerted Sandoval to the change.

Savannah State University officials have not responded to multiple requests for comment. However, someone at the university told NewsChannel 13 that the school was not responsible for the error. Bryant & Stratton College officials also have not responded to a request for comment.

Meanwhile, Jeha said Sandoval is being treated like a criminal by the Department of Homeland Security.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

“The $20,000 bond and ankle monitor is excessive and unnecessary,” said Jeha, who is based in Syracuse. “He is a superstar on the team. He has a public persona. He’s not hiding. What they are doing is completely wrong.”

He said Sandoval remains fearful he could be re-arrested.

“I fear (agents) will come back and do something against me,” he said. “I can’t leave the house alone.”

Jeha plans to accompany him to check in with immigration officials in Malta this week. Jeha is also fairly confident that Sandoval will be able to return to Savannah in the fall, as that was part of his bond agreement. But he said it is unlikely Sandoval will be able to work out or play baseball if he has to continue wearing an ankle monitor.

Expecting that issues with his immigration status will be costly, his family has been seeking donations through a GoFundMe campaign.

Though the situation has been trying, Sandoval said, “Everything happens for a reason.” He said he harbors no ill will toward ICE or the guards at the detention center and that he prays for them.

“God is always with me and gives me strength,” he said. “Even though bad things happen, I know He is still there for me. I had brothers that didn’t speak to each other. We are now all talking to each other, and I am grateful for that.”

text:
Former White House chief of staff Mick Mulvaney said Monday that the Trump administration will lose a legal battle with The New York Times over journalists that reported on President Trump’s new Air Force One plane.

“My guess is, the administration will lose this. I’m not sure what the basis is for a lawsuit. Was there a national security leak? I have no idea. Again, I can’t leak anything because I don’t know anything, now, about it,” Mulvaney told NewsNation’s Connell McShane on “NewsNation Live.”

“I just know how it works generally, and I would be asking the exact same questions The New York Times was asking. So look, look when Trump, you know, when he gets upset, he lashes out, and I understand that,” added Mulvaney, who is a contributor to NewsNation.

Earlier this month, the Trump administration hit four Times journalists with subpoenas in the wake of the newspaper publishing a story outlining risks involving the security of the new Air Force One plane gifted to the president by Qatar. The plane just recently entered service for the administration.

The Times reported that the jet did not have some of the advanced security measures of the older aircraft used for the president’s transportation.

Julian E. Barnes, Eric Lipton, Tyler Pager and Eric Schmitt were among the reporters hit with the subpoenas. The reporters earlier that week wrote that a security precaution resulted in the president leaving a NATO summit in Turkey on the old Air Force One.

The Times journalists were called to testify before a federal grand jury in New York City “in regard to an alleged violation of federal criminal law.”

The Department of Justice (DOJ) was also reportedly trying to get ahold of the communications records of Times journalists and their families, with the outlet reporting Monday that the department had sought third-party communications companies’ records including “calls and messages on the phones of two of the reporters’ spouses” and a reporter’s mother.

text:
The Mexican man who officials say was killed by a truck last week in St. Augustine, Florida, while running from immigration officers was identified by a farmworkers’ advocacy group as a father of two on vacation with a valid tourist visa.

Juan Jairo Coronilla Duran, 28, was visiting from his hometown of San Luis de La Paz, a small city in the central state of Guanajuato, according to Orlando-based non-profit Colectivo Árbol. Officials have yet to confirm his identity.

Isaret Jeffers, who represents the organization and has been providing support to his wife, Jessica Alamilla, said Coronilla Duran arrived in the United States three weeks ago for vacation, and had only been in Florida for two days. He was hit and killed by the truck on July 14.

“He was going to return this past Saturday. He had already bought a flight,” Jeffers said. “Now, unfortunately, if he is returning, his return is different.”

The Florida Highway Patrol told the Miami Herald last week that the agency found he had been running from an encounter with Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Homeland Security Investigations agents. DHS has not provided new details since the incident took place last week.

His was the third death following an encounter with immigration officials in a week, after federal agents shot and killed Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, a Mexican man in Houston on July 7, and Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, a Colombian man, in Biddeford, Maine on July 13. Neither of the men were the targets of the agents.

As the Trump Administration carries out a sweeping mass deportation campaign, agents are rounding up immigrants on sidewalks, highways and in homes, some with work permits and other legal documentation. U.S. citizens have also been stopped and detained.

Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum has opened an investigation into the deaths of at least 18 Mexican nationals since Trump assumed office, some of whom died during arrests and others in immigration detention. She said her government wants to file criminal charges.

“We express our deepest solidarity and sincere condolences to the family of the victims. Their pain is shared by the entire nation,” Sheinbaum said on July 14. “No fellow citizen should be unprotected when facing possible abuse from authority, disproportionate use of force, or human rights violations.”

A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security declined to provide further details of last week’s incident in St. Augustine.

“On July 14, DHS law enforcement conducted an operation near St. Johns, Florida. Florida Highway Patrol and HSI are investigating an incident resulting in the death of a Mexican national,” read a statement sent again to the Herald on Monday. “We will provide an update when available.”

Coronilla Duran’s wife found out about his death while watching television, Jeffers said. Alamilla declined a request to be interviewed, and Jeffers said she is focused on returning home with his body.

Alamilla hadn’t heard from her husband in more than a day when she saw the news that a man had been killed, and feared it was him. The couple have been married for 10 years and have a seven-month-old daughter and a seven-year-old son, Jeffers said. They own a small business in San Luis de La Paz.

Alamilla flew to Florida on Friday to make arrangements with a local funeral home, Jeffers said, while relatives watched their children. On Monday, she worked with the Mexican consulate to take his body back home to Mexico.

Of the Mexicans who have died in ICE custody or during arrests, at least four died by presumed suicide, including 19-year-old Royer Perez-Jimenez in March in Florida.

Jeffers said that Colectivo Árbol mainly supports farmworkers, many of whom are afraid to leave their homes amid immigration arrests.

“People are too afraid to go out and do things that used to be normal, like going to the supermarket, taking their kids to the park,” Jeffers said. “None of that is happening anymore.”

Unmarked blue SUVs

Jose Rivera, a truck driver for a garbage collection company, witnessed Coronilla Duran run out of the gas station in front of a Wawa convenience store off the highway.

Rivera had stopped for breakfast, and was sitting in his truck parallel to the highway just before 7 a.m. Coronilla Duran wore a light sky blue hoodie over a white T-shirt, blue jeans and Timberland shoes, he said.

Coronilla Duran ran to the sidewalk leading to State Road 16 and turned around. Rivera followed Coronilla Duran’s gaze in his truck’s rearview mirror to see what he was running from.

“That’s when I see the undercover car with the lights on,” Rivera said. “But when I looked back, he started running across the road.”

Rivera said he saw unmarked blue SUVs with tinted windows stopped on either side of a car at the gas station, and one moved to follow Coronilla Duran. The agents were in green uniforms, he said, and he thought they were from St. Johns County Sheriff’s Office. But the sheriff’s office told the Herald it wasn’t involved in the incident, and responded later to investigate the traffic accident.

Rivera said Coronilla Duran reached the median of the highway, a small strip of grass, slipped and fell, picked himself up, and stumbled onto the asphalt of the other lane of traffic.

“The traffic was coming pretty quick, and he just lost his footing and didn’t look where the traffic was coming,” Rivera said. “He kept looking back.”

Rivera watched as the man fell in front of a trailer-tractor, and knew instantly that he had died.

Agents didn’t notice at first, Rivera thought, because he saw an officer point to the woods on the other side, as if they thought he escaped. But then they noticed the body in the road.

“It was a heartbreaking moment for me,” Rivera said. “I have kids around his age.”

Officers began to close off the road, and Rivera drove off. When he later heard the man’s age he found it hard to believe. He looked younger, in the brief second Rivera glimpsed his face.

“I hate when things like that happen, especially to young ones,” Rivera told the Herald. “I’m almost 60, and yeah, you know, I’ve been through a lot of life, but everybody should make it until they’re older, right?”
